steps.observation: Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
# The Last Light

Old Thomas had kept the light burning for thirty-one years.

Every evening, as the sun melted into the Atlantic, he climbed the iron staircase — eighty-two steps, he knew without counting — and lit the lamp. Every morning, he descended and made his coffee, black, in a dented tin pot that had belonged to his father.

He didn't mind the solitude. People assumed he must, but they were wrong. The sea was company enough, and it had better conversations than most men he'd known. It argued and whispered and sometimes fell into a long, thoughtful silence that Thomas deeply respected.

One October night, a storm arrived without much warning. The wind came sideways, and the rain hit the glass like handfuls of gravel. Thomas sat in his chair at the top of the tower, watching the light sweep its slow circle across the chaos below, and he felt, as he always did in bad weather, entirely useful.

Then he saw it. A shape in the water. A small vessel tilting badly, maybe a quarter mile out.

He grabbed his radio and called the coast guard. Then he stood at the glass and did the only thing he could — he kept watch. He bore witness. He made sure the light kept turning.

An hour later, three fishermen sat in his kitchen, wrapped in wool blankets, warming their hands on mugs of black coffee.

"We saw the light," one of them said. "We just kept rowing toward the light."

Thomas nodded and refilled their cups.

He didn't think of himself as a hero. Heroes did extraordinary things. He had simply done what he always did — shown up, climbed the stairs, and kept the lamp burning.

Which, he supposed, was the whole point.
